title: On-chip Quantum Measurement of Squeezing Generated from a Silicon Nitride Micro-ring Resonator
authors: Yuhang Lei, Chenfei Cui, Yue Li, Hon Ki Tsang, Z. Y. Ou
abstract: Integration of quantum optical technique on-chip is crucial for large scale applications of quantum technology, which were proven in a free space environment to be superior to the corresponding classical technology. Squeezed states of light can be used for enhancing the sensitivity of quantum sensors and for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Although chip-based squeezed light generation has advanced significantly, practical impact remains limited because coupling losses between the chip and off-chip detectors destroy delicate quantum correlations, restricting the amount of observed squeezing. Here, we overcome this limitation by implementing the idea of on-chip quantum measurement with the aid of a parametric amplifier and applying it to the squeezed state generated by a silicon nitride (SiN) microring resonator. In our scheme, two matched SiN micro-rings are sequentially constructed. The first ring generates a squeezed state, whereas the second ring acts as a high-gain parametric amplifier (PA) that measures the squeezed state before the light experiences significant off-chip loss. This architecture is inherently loss-tolerant: the amplifier elevates the quantum noise well above the vacuum level, making the measurement insensitive to downstream losses. We directly observe a quantum noise reduction of 4.6 dB from the first ring, despite a chip-to-fiber coupling loss exceeding 5 dB. This work also demonstrates the first monolithic SU(1,1) interferometer with an estimated 5 dB signal-to-noise enhancement compared to traditional linear interferometers, and thus establishes a practical pathway for chip-based quantum sensors.
summary: The paper addresses the critical issue of signal degradation due to coupling losses when measuring quantum light states on photonic chips. The authors propose and experimentally demonstrate an 'on-chip quantum measurement' technique using cascaded silicon nitride micro-ring resonators acting as a squeezer followed by a parametric amplifier. This method successfully measures significant squeezing (4.6 dB) even with substantial external optical loss, establishing a scalable platform for integrated quantum sensing.
main_problem: The primary challenge is that coupling losses between on-chip quantum optical components and off-chip detectors destroy fragile quantum correlations, limiting the observable squeezing.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated a 4.6 dB quantum noise reduction despite exceeding 5 dB of chip-to-fiber coupling loss by implementing an on-chip measurement scheme.
method: They utilized a two-stage system: one micro-ring resonator generates the squeezed state, and a second ring acts as a high-gain parametric amplifier (OPA) to measure this state before significant external loss occurs.
model_or_system: The physical platform is an integrated silicon nitride (SiN) photonic chip containing two cascaded micro-ring resonators. The system functions as a monolithic SU(1,1) interferometer when used for sensing.
key_observables: Quantum noise reduction (measured in dB), interference fringe visibility, and the measured squeezing level relative to vacuum noise.
important_parameters: Chip-to-fiber coupling loss (>5 dB); observed quantum noise reduction (4.6 dB); high gain regime of the OPA ($G \gg 1$).
main_assumptions: The measurement is inherently loss-tolerant because the amplifier elevates the quantum noise floor above vacuum levels, making detection insensitive to downstream losses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the conceptual schematic (Squeezer $ightarrow$ OPA), the device structure on SiN, and crucially, the measured quantum noise spectra comparing squeezed vs. vacuum states under varying pump phases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of loss in chip-based quantum optics, proposes the parametric amplifier assisted measurement scheme (SU(1,1) interferometer), details the experimental implementation on SiN rings, and presents quantitative measurements demonstrating noise reduction despite high coupling losses.
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial engineering solution to a major bottleneck in integrated quantum photonics—loss. By showing how amplification can circumvent loss limitations, it paves a practical path for scaling quantum sensors onto chips.
